newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-ALL BLACK CONNECTION THREATENS WELSH.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ALL BLACK CONNECTION THREATENS WELSH.

text.p: If Wales suffer a surprise home defeat against Ireland at Cardiff Arms Park on Saturday, one of the people they should blame is iron-willed All Black captain Sean Fitzpatrick.

Fitzpatrick, his country's most capped player, has emerged as a central reason why the Welsh front-row will find themselves facing New Zealand-born hooker Ross Nesdale when they pack down at the first scrum this weekend.

Injury to three Irish hookers originally ahead of him in the queue has catapulted the 27-year-old Nesdale into a Five Nations debut less than 12 months after leaving Auckland in frustration at being Fitzpatrick's permanent understudy at provincial level.
A former Auckland University captain, Nesdale was on the bench as Fitzpatrick's deputy when the British Lions lost 23-18 to Auckland at Eden Park in 1993 and spent four years in the same role.

Eventually in April last year he decided his future lay elsewhere and headed for Britain to join the Newcastle side being expensively assembled by Rob Andrew, keen to escape Fitzpatrick's long shadow.

"I kept waiting for him to retire at the end of each season, but he never did and he doesn't look like doing so now either," said Nesdale. "So I'm pleased I decided to come to the northern hemisphere to play rugby, to see how far I could go in the game over here."
Nesdale was born on a farm 30 miles from Palmerston North, but his grandfather hailed from County Cork in Ireland and a cousin, Tom Nesdale, won an Irish cap against France in 1961.
He has an Irish passport and insists he has "cut all ties" with New Zealand rugby, preferring to concentrate on impressing in a green jersey.
"I suppose it's not ideal to come into the team like this, to profit from the other guys' misfortunes, but that's the way it is. I'm looking forward to Saturday."

Nesdale will have the advantage of packing down alongside his club mate Nick Popplewell and needs a big game if Ireland are to continue their extraordinary record of not losing in Cardiff since 1983 and new English coach Brian Ashton is to experience a first Five Nations victory.

Much also depends on the respective number 10s, Eric Elwood and Arwel Thomas. Elwood has recovered from hamstring problems and will be seeking to recreate the form he showed on his Irish debut on the same ground four years ago in a 19-14 victory.
Thomas had an influential game against Scotland a fortnight ago, but suffered a nightmare in Dublin against the Irish last season which temporarily cost him his test place.

"Thomas is a talented footballer, and you can't afford to give him time," said Irish flanker Denis McBride. "But if you get to him and hassle him, which is what we did last year, it could put him off, though he's probably a more composed player now."
